title: IB History Past Papers: A Final-Weeks Strategy
summary: IB History past papers become a focused final-weeks plan: practise under time, apply the markscheme, log errors, and revisit weak topics efficiently.
body_markdown:
The final weeks of IB History revision are not the moment to collect more material. They are the moment to find out whether you can turn what you know into marks under pressure.


The most effective approach is a simple loop: complete an exam paper under realistic time limits, mark it carefully, record the reason behind every lost mark, revisit the weakest topic or skill, and attempt another targeted question. Each paper becomes a diagnosis rather than a verdict.


A student who repeats that loop is doing more than revising history. They are learning how the examination rewards historical knowledge, analysis, evidence, source evaluation and judgement.


### The final-weeks checklist


Use this sequence for every serious practice session:


- Choose a paper or question that matches your syllabus and level.
- Complete it under the correct time limit without notes.
- Self-mark using the relevant markscheme and level descriptors.
- Record factual, analytical, structural and timing errors separately.
- Revisit only the weak material revealed by the attempt.
- Rewrite one weak section or complete a similar question.
- Finish each week with a realistic timed simulation.


The principle is restraint. Do not attempt five papers quickly when one paper, marked and corrected properly, could teach you more.


### Begin with a timed attempt, not another reread


Imagine a student opening a Paper 2 question on authoritarian states. They recognise the topic and remember several relevant examples. That familiarity feels reassuring, but it does not reveal whether they can construct a comparative argument in time.


The clock does.


For the current course assessed in 2026, the official examination schedule gives students 1 hour for Paper 1 and 1 hour 30 minutes for Paper 2. HL students also sit Paper 3 for 2 hours 30 minutes. Practise according to the format that applies to your examination session, and confirm your requirements with your teacher if you are unsure.


Your first timed attempt should be honest:


- Use no Study Notes, textbook or prepared essay plan.
- Follow the real paper instructions.
- Write complete answers rather than bullet-point approximations.
- Stop when the allocated time ends.
- Mark unfinished work as unfinished instead of quietly extending the session.


This can feel uncomfortable. That discomfort is useful information. It exposes whether you lose time interpreting sources, planning essays, recalling precise evidence or writing conclusions.


Students who need a broader framework can use the[realistic plan for earning a 7 in IB History](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-get-a-7-in-ib-history) to connect these timed sessions with their remaining revision schedule.


### Read the IB History markscheme as feedback


A markscheme is not merely an answer sheet. It is a description of what the examiner can reward.


After finishing a paper, mark it in two passes. In the first pass, identify whether the required historical knowledge and task demands are present. In the second, examine the quality of your argument, evidence and evaluation.


For an essay, ask:


- Did the thesis answer the exact command term?
- Did each paragraph advance an argument rather than narrate events?
- Was evidence specific enough to support the claim?
- Were alternative interpretations or counterarguments considered?
- Did the conclusion make a reasoned judgement?


The IB History markscheme often uses holistic level descriptors. That means an essay may not lose one isolated mark for every flaw. Instead, its overall qualities place it within a level. Be cautious about awarding yourself the highest plausible mark. If your response sits between two levels, identify what is missing from the stronger one.


For Paper 1, examine each question separately because source comprehension, comparison, evaluation and synthesis require different skills. For essay papers, RevisionDojo’s guide to[building a 7-worthy IB History essay structure](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-history-essay-structure-7-worthy-response) helps you distinguish genuine argument from a sequence of facts.


### Keep an error log that changes your next session


Without an error log, practice can become repetitive. A student writes several essays, notices that the marks remain similar, and responds by writing even more essays. The real weakness may never be addressed.


Create a log with one entry for every important lost mark:


Error type What to record Next action


Knowledge Missing event, date, policy or example Review the relevant Study Notes and test recall


Analysis Evidence was stated but not connected to the argument Rewrite the paragraph using explicit reasoning


Question focus Response drifted away from the command term Replan the question and annotate its key terms


Source skill Origin or purpose was discussed without linking to value or limitation Practise one focused source evaluation


Structure Paragraphs repeated the same claim Build a comparative or thematic plan


Timing Final answer or conclusion was rushed Set checkpoints for planning and writing


Do not write vague entries such as “needs more detail.” Record the specific problem: “I mentioned collectivisation but did not explain how resistance limited its short-term success.” Specific errors create specific revision tasks.


Two students preserve a corrected revision mistake in a museum exhibit


*Two students preserve a corrected revision mistake in a museum exhibit.*


After several attempts, patterns will emerge. Perhaps your factual recall is strong, but your paragraphs become descriptive. Perhaps you evaluate individual sources well but struggle to integrate them into the final Paper 1 response. Your log turns a large syllabus into a short list of fixable problems.


### Revisit weak topics with active recall


Once a paper reveals a gap, resist the temptation to reread an entire chapter. Narrow the repair.


If you forgot the consequences of a policy, review that section in your Study Notes and convert the key details into Flashcards. If you could not compare two leaders, build a small thematic grid covering aims, methods, opposition and outcomes. If your argument lacked balance, ask AI Chat to challenge the logic of your plan, then verify every historical claim against your course materials.


RevisionDojo’s guide to the[best IB History resources for self-study](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-history-resources-self-study) can help you choose the right tool for each weakness. The goal is not to revisit everything. It is to repair the exact failure exposed by practice.


Then test the repair quickly. Complete a similar paragraph, source question or essay plan without notes. Improvement becomes visible only when you can retrieve and apply the material independently.


### Move from targeted IB History practice to full simulation


Not every session needs to reproduce the entire examination. Early in the final weeks, isolated questions are often more efficient because they let you work repeatedly on a weak skill.


Use the[IB History Paper 2 Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-history/ib-history-paper-2-750-1500/questionbank) to select prompts by topic and practise difficult command terms. One day might focus on planning three comparative essays. Another might involve writing two introductions and one complete body paragraph. Grading tools can provide an additional feedback layer, although teacher guidance and the official assessment criteria should remain central.


As the exam approaches, increase realism. Sit complete papers in Exam mode, remove distractions, use only permitted materials and follow the real stopping time. RevisionDojo’s guide to[IB History mock exams and practice tests](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/preparing-for-ib-history-with-mock-exams-and-practice-tests) explains how full simulations develop pacing and decision-making.


A sensible progression is:


- Begin with targeted questions and untimed planning.
- Move to timed individual responses.
- Combine questions into complete paper sections.
- Finish with full Mock Exams or Predicted Papers in Exam mode.


The simulation is not complete when the timer ends. Mark it, update the error log and schedule the next repair task immediately.


### Turn every paper into the next decision


The last weeks are too valuable for revision that merely feels productive. A completed paper matters only when it changes what you do next.


The student who began with a rushed conclusion may discover that the real problem was an overlong plan. After setting stricter checkpoints, the next essay is finished. The error log then reveals a different issue, perhaps weak comparative analysis. That becomes the next target.


This is how marks are built: attempt, mark, diagnose, repair and retest.

In the final stretch, sit timed papers in Exam mode and treat every mistake as an instruction for the next session.
